bibliographic.title: Governance, Risk, and Regulation: A Framework for Improving Efficiency in Kenyan Pension Funds
bibliographic.citation_apa: Namagwa, S. W. (2025). Governance, Risk, and Regulation: A Framework for Improving Efficiency in Kenyan Pension Funds. Journal of Financial Risk Management, 14(4), 428-455. https://doi.org/10.4236/jfrm.2025.144023

methodology.study_design: quantitative panel regression on secondary data
methodology.sample_description: seven-year secondary dataset of 128 Kenyan pension schemes
methodology.technology_context: corporate governance, board of trustees, risk management, and industry regulation in pension schemes; no AI, LLM, generative AI, chatbot, agent, or conversational system technology mentioned

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study examines corporate governance, risk management, and industry regulation effects on pension scheme efficiency in Kenya; it does not address conversational AI, LLMs, generative AI, chatbots, agents, RAG, guardrails, or governance of language-model-based systems.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Keyword overlap on governance, risk, compliance, accountability, and regulated financial context produced a false-positive triage score. The article's governance focus is institutional board governance of pension funds, not conversational or LLM governance in regulated AI systems.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal based on abstract and introductory excerpts only. Methodological quality appears adequate for its own research question on pension governance efficiency, but the study is out of scope for conversational LLM governance.

cerqual.explanation: High confidence in exclusion: provided text clearly describes a quantitative pension governance study with no conversational AI or LLM content. Relevance to the review topic is negligible despite regulated financial sector context.

coding.theme: Corporate governance and risk management in pension funds
coding.subtheme: Board composition and regulation effects on pension scheme efficiency

synthesis.main_claim: Employee representatives on the board and effective risk management have a significant positive effect on Kenyan pension scheme efficiency, while independent board members exhibit a significant negative effect; industry regulation showed no significant effect in the joint model.
synthesis.contribution: Empirical panel regression evidence linking governance and risk management factors to pension scheme efficiency in Kenya, with a proposed Agency Theory extension via a self-cleaning mechanism for elected employee trustees.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude. No usable evidence for conversational governance, LLM systems, or generative AI in regulated environments; only peripheral overlap via generic governance and financial regulation terminology.

evidence.claim: Study uses quantitative panel regression on Kenyan pension scheme data
evidence.excerpt: Using a quan- titative design, we conducted a panel regression analysis on a seven-year sec- ondary dataset of 128 Kenyan pension schemes, totalling 896 observations.

evidence.claim: Research focus is corporate governance, risk management, and industry regulation in pension schemes
evidence.excerpt: examining the combined effects of corporate governance, risk management, and industry regulation on pension scheme efficiency in Kenya

evidence.claim: No conversational AI or LLM technology is discussed
evidence.excerpt: Pension schemes' governance should prioritise the adequacy of pension payouts

evidence.claim: Governance terminology refers to corporate/board governance, not AI governance
evidence.excerpt: CG catalyses the interplay of mixt factors that define the effectiveness of the board in designing oversight tools and their costs to promote trust, accountability, transparency

evidence.claim: Regulated financial domain is pension funds in Kenya
evidence.excerpt: Governance lapses in pension schemes not only expose scheme members to old age hardship, but also dampen the public trust in the pen- sion systems.

evidence.claim: Key empirical findings on board and risk factors
evidence.excerpt: the presence of employee representatives on the board and effective risk management have a significant positive effect on efficiency. Conversely, independent board members exhibit a significant neg- ative effect.

evidence.claim: Industry regulation showed no significant effect on efficiency
evidence.excerpt: Other factors, including top management representation, female board members, and industry regulation, showed no significant effect on effi- ciency in the joint model.

evidence.claim: Theoretical contribution extends Agency Theory for pension trustees
evidence.excerpt: the electoral process for employee board members may introduce a "self-cleaning mechanism" that progressively enhances scheme efficiency. This mechanism offers a novel theoretical extension of Agency Theory
